Yeah, a lot of Gameboy titles there. That little system got me into a lot of series. I can't say I keep up to date with all of them--Pokemon, for instance, is just not the same anymore. The fifth generation-onwards has felt kinda forced, though I did like the megas in Gen VI. I've actually found that I prefer the weird mechanics and heavy glitch presence in Gens I and II more now than the base experience of most of the series.

That being said, glitches and weird mechanics were a good deal of the reason why Metroid II was the series black sheep for the longest time. Both of its remakes are great games, but I think I prefer AM2R overall. It's a bit hard going back to the GB original once you've played either of the remakes. And before I move on, since I played the DX version of Link's Awakening, I never was able to pull off the screen teleportation trick. I kept trying, but it turns out they removed it from the GBC version and didn't tell anybody.

Yes, I know the Gameboy Turok II is a bad game. However, that's how I was introduced to the Turok series and it seemed fun at the time. It was only way later that I played the N64 version of the original and found out just what I was missing.

Originally, I was introduced to DWM by a friend who was also into Pokemon (who wasn't, at the time? It was a major boom) I was confused when I met one of the random wandering NPCs who said something about "keeping your sword sharp", because I was just playing a monster-raising simulator, but that led me into looking more into Dragon Warrior as a whole and I'm glad it did. My first introduction to the series proper was Dragon Warrior III on GBC, but Monsters was where it initially started.

Donkey Kong '94 was just a treat. Originally, it just seemed like a portable black and white version of the original arcade game, but once you beat those first few levels, the entire world expanded and you see Mario unlocking new moves for each new world. I suppose this one was more of an introduction to the Mario & Donkey Kong series, but it served to introduce me to Donkey Kong as a character. Eventually I got a hold of Donkey Kong Land (yes, the ugly-ass port/sequel to Donkey Kong Country) and got into the DKC series. I still hold that the GB version of Gangplank Galleon is better than the SNES one: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZrzYc1ZxILw

While I did enjoy Mario Land I and II, it was Wario's first game, the third Mario Land game, that I really liked. Wario Land II was even better, I think, but the first game was excellent and also had that infinite life trick (I think it was start, then press select 26 times while holding B or something like that, to get extra lives, and it could be repeated as often as you wanted). I never did play Wario Land III until way later, and while I do like obtaining new powers as I go through a game, the fact that Wario started off with all of these powers in the first two games but you have to unlock them in III kinda rubbed me the wrong way.

I honestly had no idea I liked dark gothic horror stuff until the GBA had come out and I saw the preview for Circle of the Moon in a Nintendo Power. Once I finally got the system myself and started playing the game, I knew I found a new main interest. It was actually because of CotM that I first read Dracula, which was my favorite book there for a while. For the record, my first introduction to classic Castlevania came not too long afterwards, when I found out how to emulate the SNES on PC (pretty early days there, so it was shitty emulation) and played Super Castlevania IV.

Not long after I got my first GBA, I was looking for more new games and I ended up getting Lufia III. I think I had my eye on Golden Sun or Breath of Fire, but I hadn't bothered reading the title or looking at the sidebar of the box I picked up and ended up with this GBC game instead. I think it turned out for the best, though, because I played the shit out of that game, and subsequently found out about its much more lauded predecessor because of it (so yes, Lufia II was among my first emulated SNES games as well).

My first introduction to Sonic was actually that dumbass cartoon with Scratch and Grounder. I enjoyed it well enough at the time (I was fucking 5, give me a break), but it wasn't until my family went to an internet cafe (which was actually pretty unusual in my area, even at the time) that I was introduced to Earthworm Jim and Sonic CD on the PC. We eventually got both games (several years later, we didn't even have a home PC for a good while, let alone one per person), but I preferred Sonic over Earthworm Jim (although Earthworm Jim had those PC cheats you could use if you were clever). On that note, a few years after that we also got Spider-Man, which had its own set of cheats you could type in (man, the N64 version of that was nerfed to hell and back)--but that wasn't my introduction to Spider-Man, so I guess it's irrelevant here.

Anyway, I think it was a little before getting either of those CD games that I first got Doom. We picked it up in an airport (yes, it was the shareware version, but my idiot parents paid for it anyway). I've never been real into FPS games, but I did enjoy the little time I could with Doom (had to share the family computer, after all). I think if I had been able to spend more time with it, I would've discovered Turok properly rather than through a shitty GB game with the name slapped on it.

I actually ended up with Goldeneye 007 by happenstance. I'd just seen Majora's Mask for the first time at a sleepover and I begged my parents for an N64. They bought one off of eBay and it came with this James Bond game. I'd only seen little bits of 007 movies at a friend's house before, and the spy thing was cool, but the first person thing didn't feel right to me at the time. However, I gave it a go and found fun there. Even better was the fact that, once again, there were weird cheat codes in the game. I actually got my sister (who never really got into computers at all) to play a bit with me, using both DK mode and paintball mode.

I've got to say, though, purely from a gameplay perspective, the job system in V is probably the best executed.
